content: Insulin aspart is a synthetic, short-acting form of human insulin used to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with type 1 diabetes, where the body does not produce insulin, and in some individuals with type 2 diabetes, where the body does not use insulin effectively. It facilitates the movement of glucose from the bloodstream into tissues for energy and inhibits the liver from producing additional glucose. This medication is administered as a subcutaneous injection, typically 5 to 10 minutes before meals. It can also be delivered via an external insulin pump. It is crucial to follow your doctor’s instructions precisely and not to alter the dose or frequency without medical advice. Insulin aspart is often used in combination with longer-acting insulins. If mixed with NPH insulin, insulin aspart should be drawn into the syringe first and injected immediately. When used in an insulin pump, it must not be diluted or mixed with other solutions. Insulin aspart does not cure diabetes but helps control it, so it is important to continue using it even if you feel well. Do not switch brands or types of insulin without consulting your doctor. Insulin aspart is available in vials, cartridges for dosing pens, and prefilled pens. If using vials, syringes are required. If using cartridges, you will need a compatible insulin pen. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions for your device and ask your healthcare provider for guidance if needed. Never reuse or share needles, syringes, cartridges, or pens. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant container as instructed by your healthcare provider. Before injecting, inspect the insulin aspart solution. It should be clear, colorless, and free of particles. Do not use it if it appears cloudy, discolored, or expired. When preparing a dose from a vial, follow these steps: wash your hands, clean the vial stopper with alcohol, draw air into the syringe equal to your dose, inject the air into the vial, and then draw the correct dose of insulin. Remove air bubbles from the syringe before injecting. For injection, clean the skin with alcohol, pinch or spread the skin, insert the needle, and administer the dose as instructed. Rotate injection sites within the same general area to avoid using the same site more than once a month. If using an insulin pump, change the tubing, needle, and injection site every 48 hours. Inform your doctor if you are allergic to insulin or other medications, or if you are taking any prescription or over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or supplements. Certain medications, such as ACE inhibitors, beta blockers, diuretics, and others, may interact with insulin aspart. Notify your doctor if you have a history of nerve damage, kidney disease, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, consult your doctor. Follow your doctor’s dietary and exercise recommendations. Alcohol can lower blood sugar levels, so discuss safe alcohol consumption with your doctor. If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember if it is close to mealtime. If significant time has passed, contact your doctor for guidance. Do not double your dose to compensate for a missed one. Insulin aspart may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), such as shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, headache, or hunger, and treat it promptly with a sugar-containing food or drink. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness, requiring immediate medical attention. Symptoms of hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) include extreme thirst, frequent urination, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can result in diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition with symptoms such as fruity-smelling breath, nausea, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Common side effects of insulin aspart include redness, swelling, or itching at the injection site, as well as changes in skin texture. Serious side effects, such as a full-body rash, shortness of breath, or rapid heartbeat, are rare but require immediate medical attention. Report any unusual side effects to your doctor or the FDA’s MedWatch program. Store unopened insulin aspart in the refrigerator, but do not freeze it. If refrigeration is unavailable, store it at room temperature away from heat and sunlight, and use it within 28 days. Opened vials can be stored in the refrigerator or at room temperature for up to 28 days. Opened cartridges and pens should be kept at room temperature and not refrigerated. Discard any insulin exposed to extreme temperatures or that is expired. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal methods. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Symptoms of overdose include severe hypoglycemia, confusion, or loss of consciousness. Keep all medical appointments and monitor your blood sugar and HbA1c levels as directed by your doctor. Adjustments to your insulin dose may be necessary during illness, stress, or changes in diet or activity level. Wear medical alert identification indicating you have diabetes. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refills.
